title: Job 2:1–6
context: The narrator returns to the heavenly scene. Again God’s sons present themselves before the LORD, and Satan comes among them to present himself. The LORD again commends Job as a blameless and upright servant, now adding that Job still maintains his integrity, “although you incited me against him, to ruin him without cause.” Satan answers with “Skin for skin” and asks that Job’s bone and flesh be touched, predicting that he will renounce God to his face. The LORD places Job in Satan’s hand, with a new limit: “Only spare his life.” The speakers are the narrator, the LORD, and Satan. WEB’s “Satan” and “God’s sons” are to be handled as in 1:6–12: a title or a name remains hedged, and God’s sons are heavenly beings, with stronger identifications held loosely. The permission-versus-decree difference at 2:6 should be treated fairly in the regular notes, as at 1:12, and should point again to Judges 9:23 and to the census notes at 2 Samuel 24:1 and 1 Chronicles 21:1, not to a new keyContrast. Shared ground remains explicit: God is not the author of evil; Satan acts only within the limit now reset, Job’s life spared; and Job has not been, and will not be, charged with sin (1:22; 2:10). The ruin “without cause” is the LORD’s own word that this is not punishment for Job’s guilt. Both traditions read the unit as a second heavenly grant, narrower in one respect and heavier in another.

verses.text: Again, on the day when God’s sons came to present themselves before the LORD, Satan came also among them to present himself before the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
The narrator says, “Again, on the day when God’s sons came to present themselves before the LORD, Satan came also among them to present himself before the LORD.” The scene of 1:6 is repeated, now with the added notice that Satan comes to present himself before the LORD. The same hedges apply: God’s sons are heavenly beings; Satan is WEB’s wording, and whether the term is a title or a name is not settled here.

Arminian readers take the second gathering as a real return of the same court, not a mere literary double of the first scene.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also read a second presentation before the LORD, the adversary again among God’s sons, the book’s own frame for what will now be asked.

Both traditions keep the identifications hedged, as in 1:6, and invent no contrast over the repeated opening.

verses.text: The LORD said to Satan, “Where have you come from?” Satan answered the LORD, and said, “From going back and forth on the earth, and from walking up and down in it.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD asks, “Where have you come from?” Satan answers, as in 1:7, “From going back and forth on the earth, and from walking up and down in it.” The exchange is almost the same as the first. It still does not imply that the LORD is seeking information he lacks. Classical Arminians affirm exhaustive foreknowledge and are not to be read as open theists; Reformed readers likewise deny ignorance in God.

Arminian readers hear the repeated question as the court being opened again, God already knowing both the adversary’s path and Job’s stand.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also refuse to treat the question as a gap in God’s knowledge. The same going to and fro is reported, and the LORD will again be the one who names Job.

Both traditions keep the dialogue consistent with 1:7, without a contrast over divine knowledge.

verses.text: The LORD said to Satan, “Have you considered my servant Job? For there is no one like him on the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil. He still maintains his integrity, although you incited me against him, to ruin him without cause.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD again names “my servant Job” as “a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil”. Job still maintains his integrity, “although you incited me against him, to ruin him without cause.” The commendation of 1:8 is repeated, then sharpened, and the ruin has been “without cause” as to Job’s guilt. The words “you incited me against him” are the LORD’s own wording to Satan and should be reported as such, not explained away. It is not a new keyContrast; the relation of God’s will to the adversary’s instigation belongs with Judges 9:23 and the census notes already cited. Shared ground stands: the ruin was not a punishment Job had earned, and God is not the author of evil.

Arminian readers hear the LORD confirming Job’s integrity after the first trial, and describing Satan’s instigation and the permission already given, without Job being charged with cause for the ruin.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also start from the LORD’s word: Job maintains his integrity, and he was ruined without cause. The words “you incited me” are allowed to stand in the scene, under God’s governing will, without making God the author of sin.

Both traditions take “without cause” as the book’s clear word that Job’s suffering is not a verdict on hidden guilt.

verses.text: Satan answered the LORD, and said, “Skin for skin. Yes, all that a man has he will give for his life.
verses.arminianNotes:
Satan answers, “Skin for skin. Yes, all that a man has he will give for his life.” The speaker is Satan. The proverb-like opening is his, and the point is that a man will surrender goods to keep his life. The notes do not pretend to a more certain origin of the saying than the verse itself supplies. The accusation is now aimed at Job’s person, not only at what he had.

Arminian readers take the line as a further slander: Satan still denies that Job’s fear of God is disinterested, and now presses the issue to life itself.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave “Skin for skin” in the accuser’s mouth, a claim about self-preservation, not the narrator’s doctrine, and not already a verdict on Job.

Both traditions refuse to grant the charge in advance, and they invent no contrast over the proverb.

verses.text: But stretch out your hand now, and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will renounce you to your face.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The new dare is, “But stretch out your hand now, and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will renounce you to your face.” The wording matches 1:11, except that now bone and flesh, not “all that he has,” are to be touched. Satan again speaks of the LORD’s hand, and again predicts a public renouncing. The speaker is Satan; the prediction is still his.

Arminian readers hear a sharper test, aimed at Job’s body, and a repeated claim that Job will renounce God if the hedge is pulled closer.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also set the sentence beside 1:11: the same predicted renouncing, now aimed at flesh and bone, still an accusation, not the book’s conclusion.

Both traditions keep the forecast ungranted, and they wait on the limit the next verse will set.

verses.text: The LORD said to Satan, “Behold, he is in your hand. Only spare his life.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “Behold, he is in your hand. Only spare his life.” Job himself is now placed in Satan’s hand, with one express reserve: his life is to be spared. Shared ground should be restated. God is not the author of evil. Satan may act only within this new limit. Job is still not charged with sin. As at 1:12, Arminian readers typically describe this as permission, God allowing and bounding the adversary’s action, with exhaustive foreknowledge, without God doing the evil of the sores. Reformed readers typically describe it as God’s sovereign will governing the adversary as a secondary agent, in the terms already discussed at Judges 9:23 and at 2 Samuel 24:1 and 1 Chronicles 21:1, while still denying that God is the author of sin. No new keyContrast should be added.

Arminian readers therefore take “he is in your hand” as a real, narrower permission, life reserved, body not reserved.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same words as a governing grant with a real bound, “Only spare his life,” with Satan remaining an agent under God, not a rival power.

Both traditions agree on the limit, on God’s holiness, and on Job’s innocence, and they point to the existing box at Judges 9:23 rather than creating another.
